# About this class

Importing and inspecting data, data manipulation, descriptive statistics, quantitative and qualitative graphs, correlation and ggplot2.

These notes are organized as a standalone R Markdown lesson. Run the code chunks in order and use **Knit** in RStudio to generate the report.

# 3. Importing, inspecting and managing data

## 3.1 Importing data

Choose the import function according to the file format.

```{r import-examples, eval=FALSE}
# CSV file
my_data <- read.csv("data/my_data.csv")

# Text file
my_text_data <- read.table("data/my_data.txt", header = TRUE)

# Excel file (install and load readxl first)
# install.packages("readxl")
library(readxl)
my_excel_data <- read_excel("data/my_data.xlsx")

# Inspect imported data
head(my_data)
tail(my_data)
str(my_data)
summary(my_data)
```

Replace the example paths with the actual locations of your files. For Windows paths, use forward slashes or escaped backslashes.

## 3.2 Useful inspection functions

```{r inspect-data}
data("airquality")
head(airquality)
tail(airquality)
dim(airquality)
names(airquality)
str(airquality)
summary(airquality)
```

Useful functions:

- `head()` – first rows.
- `tail()` – last rows.
- `dim()` – number of rows and columns.
- `names()` – variable names.
- `str()` – structure and data types.
- `summary()` – descriptive summaries.
- `length()` – number of elements in a vector.

## 3.3 Selecting rows and columns

```{r selecting-data}
head(airquality, 6)
airquality[1:5, ]       # First five rows
airquality[, "Temp"]    # One column
airquality[10:20, ]     # Rows 10 to 20
airquality[, -1]        # All columns except the first
airquality$Wind         # Select a column using $
```

## 3.4 Combining data

`cbind()` combines objects column-wise. The number of rows must match. `rbind()` combines objects row-wise, and the columns must be compatible.

```{r combining-data}
data_a <- data.frame(x = 1:3, group = c("A", "B", "C"))
data_b <- data.frame(z = 3:1)

cbind(data_a, data_b)

new_row <- data.frame(x = 10, group = "D")
rbind(data_a, new_row)
```

## 3.5 Creating a new variable

The BMI formula is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.

```{r create-variable}
# Example data
people <- data.frame(
  HEIGHT = c(161, 155, 158, 170, 160),
  WEIGHT = c(50, 49, 42, 65, 60)
)

people$BMI <- round(
  people$WEIGHT / (people$HEIGHT / 100)^2,
  digits = 2
)

people
summary(people$BMI)
```

Prefer `data$variable` or `with(data, ...)` over `attach()`, because `attach()` can make it unclear which object a variable comes from.

## 3.6 Working with dates

```{r dates}
today <- Sys.Date()
today
format(today, "%B %d %Y")
format(today, "%A")

dob <- as.Date("2000-02-10")
difftime(today, dob, units = "days")

start_date <- as.Date("2020-02-13")
end_date <- as.Date("2021-01-22")
end_date - start_date
```

# 4. Exploratory data analysis and descriptive statistics

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) helps us understand the structure, quality, distribution and relationships in a dataset before modelling.

## 4.1 Summary statistics for quantitative variables

```{r summary-statistics}
data("mtcars")

mean(mtcars$mpg)
median(mtcars$mpg)
sd(mtcars$mpg)
var(mtcars$mpg)
min(mtcars$mpg)
max(mtcars$mpg)
range(mtcars$mpg)
quantile(mtcars$mpg)
summary(mtcars$mpg)
```

## 4.2 A reusable summary function

```{r summary-function}
summary_stats <- function(x) {
  c(
    count = sum(!is.na(x)),
    mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    standard_deviation = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    minimum = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum = max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

summary_stats(mtcars$mpg)
summary_stats(mtcars$wt)
```

## 4.3 Graphs for quantitative variables

- **Histogram:** shows the frequency distribution of one numerical variable.
- **Boxplot:** shows the median, quartiles, spread and potential outliers.
- **Density plot:** displays a smoothed estimate of a distribution.
- **Scatter plot:** examines the relationship between two numerical variables.
- **Line graph:** shows change over an ordered sequence, commonly time.

```{r quantitative-graphs, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
hist(mtcars$mpg,
     main = "Distribution of miles per gallon",
     xlab = "Miles per gallon")

boxplot(mtcars$mpg,
        main = "Boxplot of miles per gallon",
        ylab = "MPG")

plot(density(mtcars$mpg),
     main = "Density of miles per gallon")

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg,
     main = "Vehicle weight and fuel efficiency",
     xlab = "Weight",
     ylab = "Miles per gallon")
```

## 4.4 Graphs for qualitative variables

Qualitative variables describe categories. Common graphs include:

- **Bar chart:** compares category counts or proportions.
- **Pie chart:** shows each category as a share of the whole.
- **Grouped bar chart:** compares categories across groups.
- **Stacked bar chart:** shows the composition of groups.
- **Mosaic plot:** visualizes the relationship between categorical variables.

```{r qualitative-graphs, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
mtcars$cyl_factor <- factor(mtcars$cyl)

cylinder_counts <- table(mtcars$cyl_factor)
cylinder_counts

barplot(cylinder_counts,
        main = "Cars by number of cylinders",
        xlab = "Cylinders",
        ylab = "Number of cars")

pie(cylinder_counts,
    main = "Proportion of cars by cylinders")

transmission <- factor(
  mtcars$am,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("Automatic", "Manual")
)

cylinder_transmission <- table(mtcars$cyl_factor, transmission)

barplot(cylinder_transmission,
        beside = TRUE,
        legend = TRUE,
        main = "Transmission by cylinder group",
        xlab = "Number of cylinders")
```

## 4.5 Relationship between a categorical and a quantitative variable

A boxplot can compare the distribution of a numerical variable across categories.

```{r categorical-quantitative}
data(iris)

boxplot(
  Petal.Length ~ Species,
  data = iris,
  main = "Petal length by iris species",
  xlab = "Species",
  ylab = "Petal length"
)

by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, mean)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, sd)
by(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Species, summary)
```

## 4.6 Relationship between two categorical variables

A contingency table counts observations for combinations of categories.

```{r categorical-categorical}
data(UCBAdmissions)
ucba <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions)

admission_table <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucba)
admission_table

# Row proportions
prop.table(admission_table, margin = 1)

# Visualize the table
mosaicplot(admission_table,
           main = "Admission by gender",
           color = TRUE)
```

**Simpson's paradox** occurs when a trend in combined data disappears or reverses after the data are divided into meaningful subgroups. It is a reminder to examine relevant grouping variables rather than relying only on an overall comparison.

## 4.7 Correlation and scatter plots

Correlation measures the direction and strength of a linear association between two quantitative variables. Its value ranges from -1 to +1.

```{r correlation}
cor(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)

plot(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars,
     main = "Weight versus MPG",
     xlab = "Weight",
     ylab = "MPG")

abline(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars), lwd = 2)
```

Correlation does not, by itself, establish causation.

# 5. Data visualization with ggplot2

`ggplot2` builds graphs by combining a dataset, aesthetic mappings and geometric layers using the `+` operator.

```{r ggplot-setup}
# Install once if needed:
# install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)
```

## 5.1 Scatter plot

```{r ggplot-scatter, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle weight and fuel efficiency",
    x = "Weight",
    y = "Miles per gallon"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 5.2 Add a fitted regression line

```{r ggplot-regression-line, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Linear relationship between weight and MPG") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 5.3 Boxplot and histogram

```{r ggplot-box-hist, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Petal.Length)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Petal length across species") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of MPG") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 5.4 Grouping and facets

Grouping allows multiple categories to be displayed in one graph. Facets create separate panels for subsets of the data.

```{r ggplot-grouping, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
mtcars$am_label <- factor(
  mtcars$am,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("Automatic", "Manual")
)

mtcars$cyl_label <- factor(mtcars$cyl)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg, color = cyl_label)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ am_label) +
  labs(
    title = "Fuel efficiency by horsepower and transmission",
    x = "Horsepower",
    y = "Miles per gallon",
    color = "Cylinders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 5.5 Useful ggplot2 geometries

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `geom_bar()` | Bar chart |
| `geom_col()` | Bar chart using supplied values |
| `geom_boxplot()` | Boxplot |
| `geom_density()` | Density plot |
| `geom_histogram()` | Histogram |
| `geom_jitter()` | Adds small position adjustments to points |
| `geom_line()` | Line graph |
| `geom_point()` | Scatter plot |
| `geom_smooth()` | Adds a fitted smooth or model line |
| `geom_violin()` | Violin plot |
| `geom_text()` | Adds text labels |
